title: 2002 HMMT February Calculus Problem 9
statement: Suppose \(f\) is a differentiable real function such that \(f(x)+f^{\prime}(x) \leq 1\) for all \(x\), and \(f(0)=0\). What is the largest possible value of \(f(1)\) ? (Hint: consider the function \(e^{x} f(x)\).)

solutions.text: \(1-1 / e\) Let \(g(x)=e^{x} f(x)\); then \(g^{\prime}(x)=e^{x}\left(f(x)+f^{\prime}(x)\right) \leq e^{x}\). Integrating from 0 to 1 , we have \(g(1)-g(0)=\int_{0}^{1} g^{\prime}(x) d x \leq \int_{0}^{1} e^{x} d x=e-1\). But \(g(1)-g(0)=e \cdot f(1)\), so we get \(f(1) \leq(e-1) / e\). This maximum is attained if we actually have \(g^{\prime}(x)=e^{x}\) everywhere; this entails the requirement \(f(x)+f^{\prime}(x)=1\), which is met by \(f(x)=1-e^{-x}\).
